abstract: |
  LLM judges can grade free-text legal exam solutions at scale, but their scores vary across judges
  and across repeated runs. Careful examiners reduce such variance with a grading sheet
  (*Bewertungsbogen*) that splits the expected solution into small steps worth a fixed number of
  points. We ask whether a sheet generated automatically from the case and its model solution
  reduces the variance of LLM grading of German law exams, and at what cost to agreement with human
  graders. In a first iteration, twelve models generated sheets for 15 exams, and judges re-graded
  45 answers with blind human grades. The sheets did not make capable judges steadier on average:
  the effect depended on the judge, the sheets cost some agreement with the human graders, and under
  the sheet several judges gave high scores to empty or copied answers. We then rebuilt the pipeline. The
  model writes small steps with requirements, the judge must support each credit with a quote from
  the answer, code allocates the points and checks every quote, and defensible alternative
  solutions and auxiliary opinions are represented explicitly. We validate it against grades of real
  exam scripts on the exam author's own sheet, benchmark which models generate good sheets and which
  use them well, and describe how such exams are graded in practice. \pending{results of the full benchmark
  and the recommended pipeline}

```{python}
MINUS = "−"


def _q(x, nd):
    """Round half up from the value's decimal form (10.85 -> 10.9), not
    from its binary float (which would give 10.8)."""
    return Decimal(repr(float(x))).quantize(Decimal(1).scaleb(-nd), rounding=ROUND_HALF_UP)


def num(x, nd=2):
    return f"{_q(x, nd):.{nd}f}".replace("-", MINUS)


def sgn(x, nd=2):
    return f"{_q(x, nd):+.{nd}f}".replace("-", MINUS)


def cor(x, nd=2):
    """Correlations and p-values without the leading zero (.77, -.13)."""
    s = f"{abs(_q(x, nd)):.{nd}f}"
    s = s[1:] if s.startswith("0") else s
    return (MINUS if x < 0 else "") + s


def pv(p):
    return cor(p, 3) if p < 0.01 else cor(p, 2)


def pct(x, nd=0):
    return f"{_q(100 * x, nd):.{nd}f}%"


def ci(c, nd=2):
    return f"95% CI {sgn(c[0], nd)} to {sgn(c[1], nd)}"


def rng(a, b, nd=1, sep="–"):
    return f"{num(a, nd)}{sep}{num(b, nd)}"


def usd(x, nd=0):
    return f"USD {x:,.{nd}f}"

def tex_escape(s):
    for a, b in (("\\", "\\textbackslash{}"), ("&", "\\&"), ("%", "\\%"), ("$", "\\$"),
                 ("#", "\\#"), ("_", "\\_"), ("{", "\\{"), ("}", "\\}")):
        s = s.replace(a, b)

def crit_tex(s):
    return tex_escape(s).replace(">=", "$\\geq$").replace("<=", "$\\leq$").replace("<", "$<$")


def write_table(name, caption, label, header, rows, colspec=None, size=r"\small", wide=False, note=None):
    """A captioned booktabs table in assets/<name>.tex, included with \\input
    (raw blocks with \\caption get mangled by Quarto's crossref pass)."""
    colspec = colspec or ("l" + "r" * (len(header) - 1))
    esc = lambda t: re.sub(r"(?<!\\)%", r"\\%", str(t))  # a bare % would start a LaTeX comment
    caption = esc(caption)
    rows = [r if r == "MIDRULE" else (esc(r) if isinstance(r, str) else [esc(c) for c in r]) for r in rows]
    lines = [r"\begin{table}[t]", rf"\caption{{{caption}}}", rf"\label{{{label}}}", r"\centering", size]
    if wide:
        lines.append(rf"\begin{{tabular*}}{{\textwidth}}{{@{{\extracolsep{{\fill}}}}{colspec}@{{}}}}")
    else:
        lines.append(rf"\begin{{tabular}}{{@{{}}{colspec}@{{}}}}")
    lines += [r"\toprule", " & ".join(header) + r" \\", r"\midrule"]
    for r in rows:
        if r == "MIDRULE":
            lines.append(r"\midrule")
        elif isinstance(r, str):
            lines.append(r + r" \\")
        else:
            lines.append(" & ".join(str(c) for c in r) + r" \\")
    lines += [r"\bottomrule", r"\end{tabular*}" if wide else r"\end{tabular}"]
    if note:
        lines += [r"\par\smallskip", rf"\parbox{{\textwidth}}{{\footnotesize {note}}}"]
    lines.append(r"\end{table}")
    (ASSETS / f"{name}.tex").write_text("\n".join(lines) + "\n", encoding="utf-8")
    print("```{=latex}\n\\input{assets/" + name + ".tex}\n```\n")
```

# Introduction {#sec-intro}

German law students learn and are examined through case solutions (*Falllösungen*). A candidate
receives a set of facts (*Sachverhalt*) and writes a legal opinion in a prescribed appraisal style
(*Gutachtenstil*). The state examinations grade such opinions on a statutory scale from 0 to
`{python} V["R18"]` points [@jurprnotskv1981]. Grading them is hard. Different examiners give the
same script different grades [@hufeld2024]. To grade consistently, correctors often build a point
scheme over the expected solution before they grade [@frenzel2011korrektur]. Many do this with a grading sheet
(*Bewertungsbogen*): the expected solution split into small steps, each worth a number of points
(*Bewertungseinheiten*, BE), and a key that maps the BE total to a grade.

Large language models (LLMs) can grade such texts at scale. On German case solutions, an LLM judge
with one rubric for all exams tracks human graders on average, but its scores vary between judges
and between repeated runs [@nagl2026bengerdata]. This paper studies the obvious remedy: let one
model write an exam-specific grading sheet from the case and its model solution (*Musterlösung*),
and let a judge model grade against it. If it works, the sheet becomes an auditable, editable
artifact between the model solution and the grade, which an examiner can read and correct.

A first iteration tested this remedy with a rich step-score sheet on `{python} V["n_exams"]` exams
with `{python} V["n_answers"]` answers and blind human grades. The sheets did not make capable judges
steadier on average, they cost some agreement with the human graders, and under the sheet several
judges gave high scores to empty or copied answers (@sec-first). We rebuilt the pipeline and ask the
question again, now also asking *which* models write good sheets and *which* use them well, against
the strongest yardstick we can get: grades of real exam scripts on the exam author's own sheet
and scale. RQ1 and RQ2 carry the story; the others explain the result.

- **RQ1 Variance.** Does grading against a generated sheet make judges steadier, across repeated
  passes, across judges and across independently generated sheets for the same exam?
- **RQ2 Validity.** How close are sheet-based grades to human grades, and to the exam author's grades
  on his own sheet and scale?
- **RQ3 Generation.** Do heterogeneous generators produce compliant, legally sound, exam-specific
  sheets under one output specification?
- **RQ4 Generator benchmark.** Which generators write the sheets that let a fixed judge grade most
  validly and reliably, and do cheap signals predict this?
- **RQ5 Judge benchmark.** Which judges use a fixed sheet best, in validity, stability, robustness to
  degenerate answers, and cost?
- **RQ6 Pipeline.** Which combination of design choices gives the lowest error against the expert
  within a cost limit?
- **RQ7 Grading practice.** How do examiners distribute points, what do they credit, where do they
  set the pass mark, how do they map points to grades, and how do they treat cardinal errors
  (*Kardinalfehler*)?

Our contributions are:

1. A grading-sheet pipeline in which the model specifies and code allocates: half-point BE,
   requirement bullets with a standard of assessment, structural forks with alternative solution
   paths, owed auxiliary opinions, and quotes verified by code (@sec-pipeline).
2. A generator benchmark with `{python} EXP["E1"]["n_generators"]` generators on
   `{python} V["n_exams"] + 1` exams, measuring sheet-sample variance and validity against human and
   expert grades (@sec-design).
3. A judge benchmark with `{python} EXP["E2"]["n_judges"][0]` to `{python} EXP["E2"]["n_judges"][1]`
   judges on fixed sheets, measuring validity, repeat variance, robustness to probes, and cost.
4. The interaction of generator and judge, and a recommended pipeline confirmed once on held-out
   expert grades.
5. An account of how German law exams are graded, co-written with an exam author (@sec-practice),
   and the defects of the first-iteration pipeline that the rebuild fixes (@sec-first,
   Appendix \ref{sec-app-corrections}).

\draftnote{contributions 2 to 4 describe experiments E1 to E4, which have not run yet; see Section 6}

The study is exploratory and was not pre-registered. Every run records the hashes of its code,
prompts and validator, and we report every run we make.

# Grading practice in German law exams {#sec-practice}

\draftnote{to be co-written with the exam author; every pending item below needs his input or experiment E6/E7}

*The setting.* The statutory scale has `{python} V["bands"]` named bands from 0 to
`{python} V["R18"]` points; `{python} V["pass_np"]` points (*ausreichend*) is the lowest pass
grade [@jurprnotskv1981]. Examiners in the state examinations grade holistically. Many first write
down the expected solution and what each part is worth [@frenzel2011korrektur]. University exams
often make this explicit: a sheet assigns BE to steps, and a key maps the BE total to the scale. Two
principles shape every sheet. A tenable solution (*vertretbare Lösung*) that is argued with sound
reasons must not be marked as wrong [@bverfge84_34]. And a consequential error (*Folgefehler*) is not
penalised twice: a later step that correctly builds on the candidate's own earlier decision still
earns credit.

*Three paradigms.* We compare three ways of grading with our instrument (Table \ref{tab:paradigms}).
The exam author's sheet (D2) is a list of steps with absolute BE, grouped into sections. Gregor
Roth's sheet for a civil-law exam (Z2) is hierarchical: its weighted items state their share of the
parent item, and each of the `{python} Z2["weighted_leaves"]` weighted leaves is graded in whole points
from `{python} num(Z2["leaf_grade_range"][0], 0)` to `{python} num(Z2["leaf_grade_range"][1], 0)`. His
grading workbook multiplies the shares down to absolute weights and averages the leaf grades with
them; its legend marks the one place where it adjusted the stated shares. A third practice is
common as well: about `{python} pct(PF["fixed_share"])` of the BE go to steps, and the grader
distributes the remaining `{python} pct(PF["free_share"])` freely, for instance for structure or the
overall impression. We do not adopt it: the free share is tied to nothing in the answer that a
second grader or a judge could check, so it invites variance and cannot be reproduced. Our
instrument keeps the half-point BE of the first paradigm, assigns every point to a step, adds
requirement bullets, lets code do the arithmetic, and can elicit the weights in the way of either
expert sheet (@sec-pipeline).

*Q1: How should the BE be distributed?* The author's sheet spreads `{python} D2["sheet"]["total_be"]`
BE over `{python} D2["sheet"]["n_steps"]` steps with at most `{python} num(D2["sheet"]["max_step_be"], 0)`
BE per step. He re-weighted some steps between runs (@sec-d2) \pending{exam author: why}. We took
the step-size guidance of
our instrument (`{python} num(GEN["step_be_guidance"][0], 1)` to `{python} num(GEN["step_be_guidance"][1], 0)`
BE per step, at most `{python} num(GEN["max_step_be"], 0)` BE) from the two expert sheets, so step
size is an input of our design, not a finding. E6 compares the BE distributions of generated sheets
with both expert sheets. \pending{BE distribution of the expert sheet and of generated sheets (E6)}

*Q2: What earns credit, including method?* In the author's sheet every step credits an issue
spotted or an argument made. No step credits a bare result; some step titles state a sub-result
instead. Our generator follows the same rule: no step may credit only an intermediate or
final result: a result earns credit only together with the reasoning that carries it, and where
several results are tenable the bullets credit the argument, not the result. Whether
method (structure, appraisal style, precise language) earns separate credit is open
\pending{exam author}. The first iteration kept style outside the points as a separate construct.
E6 compares sheets with and without method bullets.

*Q3: Where is the pass mark?* The author's key passes a script at
`{python} pct(D2["sheet"]["pass_share"])` of the BE. The platform's default key, which the
first-iteration holistic instrument also used, passes at `{python} num(KEY["pass_percent"], 0)`%.
The pass mark decides pass/fail agreement between a judge and the examiner. E6 sweeps it from
`{python} pct(EXP["E6"]["pass_mark_sweep"][0])` to `{python} pct(EXP["E6"]["pass_mark_sweep"][1])`
on stored outputs. \pending{E6}

*Q4: Is the key linear or curved?* The author's key is piecewise linear with a kink at the pass
mark: below it a grade point spans `{python} D2["sheet"]["key_be_per_grade_below_pass"]` BE, from the
pass mark upwards `{python} D2["sheet"]["key_be_per_grade_from_pass"]` BE, up to grade 18 at
`{python} D2["sheet"]["key_top_grade_be"]` BE. \pending{exam author: why this shape} The platform's
default key has the same shape: below the pass mark a grade point spans
`{python} num(KEY["mean_band_width_below_pass"], 1)` percentage points of the total on average, from
the pass mark upwards `{python} num(KEY["mean_band_width_from_pass"], 1)`. Roth's paradigm needs no
key: it averages statutory grades and passes from grade `{python} Z2["workbook"]["pass_from_grade"]`. Our rating unit
supports both views: a leaf grade maps back to BE through the exam's own key, and the weighted mean
of the leaf grades is reported next to it.

*Q5: How are cardinal errors treated?* Some errors are grave enough that examiners limit the grade
as a whole. \pending{exam author: definition, examples and expected loss} Our instrument has no such
cap yet. The consequential-error rule and the standard of each bullet decide how far an early error
propagates (@sec-judge). E6 runs `{python} EXP["E6"]["kardinalfehler_probes"]` probes with the losses
the author expects.

# Related work {#sec-related}

*Judge reliability.* Direct-scoring LLM judges [@liu2023geval; @zheng2023mtbench] correlate with
humans on average but are unreliable at the instance level: scores drift across runs
[@haldar2025rating], flip under reordering and prompt changes [@wang2024fair; @shi2024judging],
show self-preference [@panickssery2024self], and need validation against humans for each task
[@gu2024survey; @bavaresco2025llms]. Most remedies act on the judge, such as calibration or panels
[@verga2024replacing]. We act on the instrument.

*Rubrics and checklists.* Fine-grained decomposition can make evaluation more reliable: skill-wise
scoring, rubric-conditioned evaluators, atomic facts, and binary checklists that an LLM can generate
per instance [@ye2024flask; @kim2024prometheus; @hashemi2024llmrubric; @min2023factscore;
@wu2023finegrained; @lee2025checkeval; @cook2024ticking; @chen2026holistic; @gunjal2025rubrics].
These systems use binary criteria or categorical importance labels with arithmetic in code; to our
knowledge none asks the model for an exact point total, which LLMs handle poorly [@baeumel2025lookahead;
@yang2025numbercookbook]. Educational measurement finds that analytic rubrics are more reliable than
holistic scoring at a cost in rater time [@klein1998analytic; @jonsson2007use;
@brookhart2018appropriate]; an LLM rater turns that cost into inference cost. LLM essay scoring has
used fixed, exam-independent rubrics [@ke2019automated; @mizumoto2023exploring;
@stahl2024exploring], and prior decompositions carry uniform or binary weights and no doctrine of
partial credit [@kucia2026llm]. Work on attribution checks whether generated text is supported by
cited sources [@gao2023alce]; our verifier asks a narrower question, whether a quote stands in the
answer at all.

*Grading legal free text.* Legal NLP has moved from LLMs taking exams [@choi2023chatgpt;
@katz2024gpt4] to LLMs grading them with per-question structure: reasoning guidance, span-level
criteria, expert-written or official rubrics, and atomic judging [@fan2026lexam;
@chlapanis2025greekbarbench; @shi2026plawbench; @pires2025automatic; @pires2026magisbench;
@enguehard2025lemaj; @zubaer2026gradelegal; @cope2026grading]. All of them assume an
expert-written scheme. To our knowledge, no prior work generates the exam-specific point scheme,
turns tenable alternative solutions into scoreable paths, and validates the result against the
exam's author on his own sheet and scale. Empirical work on German exam grading documents low
agreement between examiners [@hufeld2024] and describes how examiners should correct
[@frenzel2011korrektur]; we add a model of the grading sheet that makes these practices explicit.

# The pipeline {#sec-pipeline}

\draftnote{describes output specification checklist-4; the D2 runs of Section 6.2 used checklist-3 (fewer validator checks, a cap message without the advice to split); frozen after E0}

The pipeline has five stages (Figure \ref{fig:pipeline}). Models do two things only. The generator
states the content of the sheet and relative weights, and the judge marks requirements and quotes
the answer. Code does everything that can be computed or checked: validation, allocation, rendering,
quote verification and aggregation. The first iteration showed why. When an earlier output
specification asked the model for exact point totals, almost no generator produced a valid sheet
\pending{yield of the exact-arithmetic specification, from the withheld sweep log}.

## Case preparation

Each exam provides a case text and a model solution. We clean both: markup escapes and tables of
contents are removed, footnotes are kept. A script is graded against the case text of its own year.

## Generation: the checklist sheet {#sec-generation}

The generator receives the case text, the model solution and a fixed output specification, the same
for every model, through plain text completion. It returns one JSON document:

- *Sections and steps.* Each step names one expected legal performance and carries a relative
  weight. Klausurschwerpunkte (the exam's focal problems) are marked groups of steps.
- *Requirement bullets.* Each step has `{python} GEN["bullets_per_step"][0]` to
  `{python} GEN["bullets_per_step"][1]` bullets, each with a relative share and a standard
  (*Maßstab*): *richtig* (judged against the correct law) or *folgerichtig* (judged against the
  candidate's own earlier decision, the consequential-error principle at bullet level). A bullet
  describes a performance that stands in the answer and can be quoted. No bullet may be met by an
  absence, none may be conditional, and none may ask only for a norm, a term or a result to be named.
  A step above `{python} num(GEN["two_bullets_above_be"], 0)` BE needs at least two bullets.
- *Forks and solution paths.* A dispute that changes only a result or its reasons stays inside a
  step as an outcome-neutral bullet. A structural fork (*Weichenstellung*) exists only where another
  tenable decision drops a step of the model solution's path or adds a step with its own
  prerequisites. Each alternative path (*Lösungsweg*) carries its own steps, the reasoning that makes
  it tenable (*Vertretbarkeitsanforderungen*), and the budget of the steps it replaces.
- *Owed auxiliary opinions.* Steps or sections can be marked as owed even when the candidate's own
  decision cuts them off (*Hilfsgutachten*), for instance when a contractual claim already fails at
  formation. The marker names the triggering decision.
- *Work results.* Each step belongs to an *Arbeitsergebnis*, such as an opinion or a draft judgment.

The model states weights, never points. How it states them is a lever with three settings: flat
weights over all steps; hierarchical shares, where each level states its share of the parent (Roth's
paradigm, Z2); and top-down BE, where the model writes section totals first and then the steps inside
(the D2 paradigm), normalized by code.

## Allocation by code {#sec-allocation}

Code turns weights into BE. It apportions `{python} GEN["half_units"]` half-units
(`{python} GEN["total_be"]` BE) over the steps by the largest-remainder (Hamilton) method
[@balinski2001fair], with a floor of `{python} num(GEN["min_step_be"], 1)` BE per step. The floor is
enforced before the remainders are ranked: steps whose quota falls below the floor are pinned to it,
and the rest is apportioned again. Every free step then lands within one half-unit of its quota
among the free steps, a
heavier step never receives less than a lighter one, and weights that already sum to the total pass
unchanged. A bullet is worth the step's BE times the bullet's share. Budgets of alternative paths
equal the sum of the steps they replace. A step above `{python} num(GEN["max_step_be"], 0)` BE fails
validation with a message that asks the model to split the step or lower its weight.

The first iteration's routine floored first and then ranked the remainders of the unfloored quotas.
An audit of its `{python} AP["n_rubrics"]` sheets found `{python} AP["as_run"]["steps_outside_fair_range"]`
steps in `{python} AP["affected_rubrics"]` sheets outside their fair range and
`{python} AP["as_run"]["order_inversion_pairs"]` order inversions in
`{python} AP["as_run"]["rubrics_with_inversion"]` sheets; `{python} AP["affected_drawn_rubrics"]` of the
`{python} AP["n_drawn"]` sheets used in the main arm was affected (Appendix \ref{sec-app-apportionment}). The
corrected routine removes both defects. On the half-point grid it also keeps distinct weights apart:
the as-run routine gave equal points to `{python} AP["as_run"]["collapsed_distinct_weight_pairs"]`
pairs of steps with different weights, the half-point routine to
`{python} AP["hamilton_half"]["collapsed_distinct_weight_pairs"]`.

## Validation and retries {#sec-validation}

A deterministic validator checks every document in two tiers (Appendix \ref{sec-app-validator}). A strict
violation fails the attempt. The model then receives its previous document and the verbatim
violation messages, for at most `{python} GEN["max_attempts"]` attempts. Strict checks cover the
structure and all cross-references, absence and conditional bullets, steps named as a result, big
steps with a single bullet, forks that replace a whole section, and paths that repeat the steps they
replace. Soft checks only log hints, for example when most steps exceed
`{python} num(GEN["step_be_guidance"][1], 0)` BE. Every sheet records content hashes of the
validator and the prompt. A lexical check cannot see paraphrase, so two steps that say the same
thing in different words pass.

## Rendering {#sec-rendering}

Code renders the sheet for the judge: sections, steps with their BE, bullets with their share in
percent and their standard, forks with their paths and tenability requirements, and notes on owed
auxiliary opinions. A second view merges consecutive steps of a section until a merged step reaches
about `{python} num(GEN["merged_view_target_be"], 0)` BE, without crossing a focal group, a fork or an
auxiliary-opinion marker. Totals do not change. The two views isolate step size as a lever.

## Judging {#sec-judge}

The judge receives four tagged inputs with fixed roles: the case, the model solution (a reference,
not the answer), the rendered sheet and the answer. It returns JSON under a schema derived from the
sheet. There are `{python} len(JDG["score_units"])` scoring units. In the *bullet* unit the judge marks
each requirement as met, partly met or not met, which code credits with
`{python} num(JDG["status_credit"]["2"], 0)`, `{python} num(JDG["status_credit"]["1"], 1)` or
`{python} num(JDG["status_credit"]["0"], 0)` of the bullet's BE. In the *step* unit it states half-point
BE per step, as on a classic sheet. In the *rating* unit it grades each step from 0 to
`{python} JDG["rating_max"]` against the statutory band definitions. Every credit needs a verbatim
quote from the answer. The judge's rules are fixed:

- *Placement.* Work counts for the step whose requirement it meets, even if it stands elsewhere in
  the same question and work result; the step is then flagged as misplaced. It counts once, and work
  on another question counts only if the answer refers to it explicitly.
- *Consequential errors.* *Folgerichtig* bullets are judged on the answer's own earlier decisions.
  Other bullets are judged on the correct law, but an error that has already cost credit is not
  charged again; the judge records the chain.
- *Auxiliary opinions.* Work on questions that the answer's own decision cut off earns credit like
  work in the main opinion. It never replaces the main result.
- *Alternatives.* In design A0 (*replace*) the judge puts the work on another tenable path onto the
  replaced steps. In the *branch* designs the judge scores every path's steps and declares, with a
  quote, which path the answer follows; a path counts as followed only if the answer argues it as its
  tenability requirements demand. A2 counts the declared path (the model solution's path if the quote
  fails), A1 the best-scoring path; one call yields both.
- *Unforeseen paths.* If the answer takes a tenable path that the sheet does not foresee, the judge
  scores the functionally corresponding step at equal depth of reasoning and flags it; such a script
  goes to human review.
- *General rules.* Contradictory results without a decision fail the requirement on the result.
  Unnecessary alternative analyses earn nothing. Length, frequent citations and strings of keywords
  are not performance, and a short, correct application meets a requirement fully.

Instructions inside the tagged inputs are ignored. A diagnosis block records the assessment status
(scored, review required, not evaluable), the work results, owed auxiliary opinions, error chains
and short hints for the candidate; it never changes points.

## Evidence verification and its limits {#sec-verifier}

Code checks every quote against the answer (Appendix \ref{sec-app-verifier}). It normalizes layout and compares
tokens in order, with small tolerances: up to `{python} VER["max_skipped_answer_words"]` skipped answer
words between quoted words, one missed quoted word per `{python} VER["one_miss_per_tokens"]`, and an
inflection or a one-letter typo on longer words. *Protected* tokens must match exactly and may never
be skipped: negations, result words and their antonyms, qualifiers, Roman numerals and every token
with a digit. A match fails when a negation or a condition stands right before it in the same
clause, or right after it in the same sentence. A fragment needs at least `{python} VER["min_tokens"]`
tokens and more than a norm citation. An unverified quote sets the item to zero; the model's own
value stays in the output for analysis.

The check has limits. It tests presence, not relevance: a real sentence can be quoted for the wrong
requirement, and only the judge decides what a sentence proves. Correct work that the judge
paraphrases instead of quoting earns nothing. A sentence that the answer copied from the case text
verifies. The edge rules also reject some correct quotes, for instance one cut before a trailing
condition that does not change the result. The first iteration had no verifier, and the platform
grades that the D2b students saw ran with an earlier version. Every arm reports its verifier version.
\pending{regression replays at the freeze: quotes re-checked on D1, D2 and the stored D2b grades, and how many flip}

## Aggregation and grades {#sec-aggregation}

A step's points are the sum of bullet credits times bullet BE (bullet unit), the stated BE (step
unit), or the BE equivalent of the step grade (rating unit): the midpoint of the grade's band under
the exam's key, with `{python} JDG["rating_max"]` points worth the full step. Code sums the unrounded
points and rounds once, half up, to the half-point grid; the step scores shown are distributed from
that total by largest remainder so that they add up to it. The grade follows from the total via the
exam's key. For the rating unit we also report the weighted mean of the step grades, Roth's
aggregation. Passes can be averaged.

```{python}
#| output: asis
lev = [
    ["Generation", "specification, validator, retries", "generator; allocation (flat, hierarchical, top-down)"],
    ["Rendering", "layout, shares in percent", "view (fine, merged)"],
    ["Judging", "rules, schema, quote check", "judge; unit (bullet, step, rating); alternatives (A0, A1, A2)"],
    ["Aggregation", "rounding, grade key", f"passes averaged ({DZ['statistics']['passes_averaged'][0]}--{DZ['statistics']['passes_averaged'][-1]}); two-judge mean"],
]
write_table(
    "tbl_levers", "Levers of the pipeline. Baselines: the first-iteration step-score sheet, the "
    "holistic instrument, and the exam author's own sheet graded by the same judge.",
    "tab:levers", ["Stage", "Fixed in code", "Levers"], lev,
    colspec="lp{0.28\\textwidth}p{0.45\\textwidth}", size=r"\footnotesize")
```

# Data and design {#sec-design}

## D1: the first-iteration corpus {#sec-d1}

D1 holds the `{python} V["n_exams"]` exams of the BenGER corpus [@nagl2026bengerdata], from civil,
public and criminal law, with `{python} V["n_answers"]` answers: per exam one traditional, one
co-created and one model-generated solution. The `{python} V["n_ann"]` human-written answers each have
grades from `{python} V["blind"]` blind raters and, un-blind, from the exam's creator; agreement uses the mean of
these `{python} V["pool"]` grades. The blind raters agree at ICC(2,1) = `{python} V["icc"]` and differ
by `{python} V["spread"]` raw points per answer on average. The prior study's primary judge tracked
the pool at $r$ = `{python} V["prior_r"]` with an MAE of `{python} V["prior_mae"]` raw points, or
`{python} V["prior_mae_np"]` grade points when the MAE is computed on the grade scale. D1 is our only data across many exams,
and its human reference is noisy.

## D2: the expert exam {#sec-d2}

D2 is one police-law exam from LMU, set in yearly runs from 2024 to 2026. Its author is a co-author
of this paper. His grading sheet has `{python} D2["sheet"]["n_steps"]` steps and
`{python} D2["sheet"]["total_be"]` BE on a half-point grid, and his key passes a script at
`{python} pct(D2["sheet"]["pass_share"])`. The sheet exists in `{python} D2["sheet"]["n_states"]`
states with the same steps: the 2024 run used earlier step maxima, and
`{python} D2["d2a"]["states"]["older_labels"]` scripts of 2025 carry older step labels; the other
2025 scripts and the 2026 run use the current sheet.

- *D2a* holds `{python} D2["d2a"]["n_scripts"]` typed scripts from the runs of 2024 (`{python} D2["d2a"]["by_year"]["2024"]`)
  and 2025 (`{python} D2["d2a"]["by_year"]["2025"]`), each
  with per-step grades on the sheet state it was graded on. We call these the *reference grades*:
  for the `{python} D2["d2a"]["grader_pending"]` scripts with older labels the grader is still being
  confirmed. The judge sees the current sheet for all scripts.
- *D2b* holds `{python} D2["d2b"]["n_uploads"]` submissions from the `{python} D2["d2b"]["year"]` run
  on our platform. We exclude `{python} D2["d2b"]["n_excluded"]` uploads from the author's own account
  (a test upload and a copy of a D2a script), leaving `{python} D2["d2b"]["n_students"]` student
  submissions. The platform graded them at submission time with GPT-5.4 Mini, and the students saw
  these grades. The author grades the `{python} D2["d2b"]["n_students"]`
  submissions blind, without access to the model grades. \pending{blind expert grades for D2b}

In total D2 has at most `{python} D2["distinct_scripts"]` distinct scripts,
`{python} D2["n_counting_dependent_pair_once"]` if one pair with overlapping text counts once. The case
text changed between runs, at least in its dates. `{python} D2["d2a"]["own_year_case_text"]` D2a
scripts are judged against their own year's text; the `{python} D2["d2a"]["later_case_text"]` scripts
of 2024 are judged against a later text and flagged. \pending{the 2024 case text from the exam author} A second grader will grade
`{python} D2["second_grader_plan"]["n_scripts"]` scripts blind (`{python} D2["second_grader_plan"]["d2a"]`
from each part) to give a human-to-human ceiling. \pending{second grader}

Before any research call to a model provider, all D2 texts are pseudonymized and checked for personal
data. The check found and removed `{python} D2["pii"]["student_name_lines_removed"]` line with a
student's name and `{python} D2["pii"]["examiner_headers_removed"]` examiner header;
`{python} D2["pii"]["grade_files_with_private_email"]` grade spreadsheets carried a private e-mail
address, which no derived file contains. The expert's sheet never reaches a generator or a holistic
judge. A canary check asserts that no prompt of any other arm contains terms of the expert sheet or
of the D2 solution.

We also hold Gregor Roth's sheet and grading workbook for a civil-law exam (Z2), without case,
solution or scripts, and use them only for their scoring format (E7).

## Experiments {#sec-experiments}

The development data are D1 and D2a. D2b is held out and used once, after the author has graded it,
to confirm the pipeline chosen on the development data. Table \ref{tab:experiments} lists the
experiments. Each runs on its own budget and only after the owner's approval.

```{python}
#| output: asis
erows = []
for e in DZ["experiments"]:
    lo, hi = e["cost_usd"]
    cost = f"{lo}" if lo == hi else f"{lo}--{hi}"
    erows.append([e["id"], e["name"], ", ".join(e["rq"]), tex_escape(e["scope"]), cost])
tot = COST["experiments_sum_usd"]

    "Experiments of the extended study, with planned costs in USD at catalog prices and "

    "tab:experiments", ["", "Experiment", "RQ", "Scope", "USD"], erows,
    colspec="lp{0.2\\textwidth}p{0.09\\textwidth}p{0.44\\textwidth}r", size=r"\footnotesize")
```

*Measures.* Against the expert we report the mean absolute error (MAE) and the signed bias of the
total, ICC(A,1) [@mcgraw1996forming], the share of grades within one grade point, and pass/fail
agreement (Cohen's $\kappa$); on D1 also the concordance correlation [@lin1989concordance] with the
human pool. Stability is the SD across repeated passes on the same sheet (*repeat SD*) and across
independently generated sheets for the same exam (*sheet-sample SD*). Robustness is the probe
battery. Faithfulness is the share of quotes the verifier rejects and the gap between the model's
total and the verified total. Cost and latency are measured per call.

*Probe battery.* Before any benchmark run, each judge and instrument passes a battery of synthetic
answers over `{python} DZ["probes"]["passes"]` passes (Appendix \ref{sec-app-probes}): negative probes (an empty
answer, the case text, another exam's solution, a keyword list, an injected instruction) must score
near zero; the exam's own model solution must score high; removing one section of the model solution
must cost about that section's BE; moving correct reasoning under another heading must cost almost
nothing.

*Estimation.* We estimate rather than test. Intervals are bootstrap CIs clustered by exam (D1) or by
script (D2); variance components come from mixed models; generator and judge ranks carry bootstrap
intervals. The data limit what we can see (Appendix \ref{sec-app-precision}). With
`{python} D2["d2a"]["n_scripts"]` D2a scripts, a paired difference in absolute error below about
`{python} num(MDE["C2_abs_error_vs_expert"]["mde"]["n_15_d2a"]["alpha_0.025"], 1)` points is not
detectable (power `{python} cor(DZ["statistics"]["mde_power"], 1)`, $\alpha$ = `{python} cor(DZ["statistics"]["mde_alpha"], 3)`, $t$-based); with all `{python} D2["distinct_scripts"]` scripts
the bound is about `{python} num(MDE["C2_abs_error_vs_expert"]["mde"]["n_38_all_distinct"]["alpha_0.025"], 1)`
points. On D1's `{python} MDE["C1_repeat_sd"]["n"]` answers a change in repeat SD below about
`{python} num(MDE["C1_repeat_sd"]["mde"]["alpha_0.025"], 2)` is not detectable. Each judge runs at the
platform's grading default temperature; we report each provider's determinism. GPT-5.6 Luna cannot be
seeded, so its repeat SD mixes sampling noise with instrument effects.

*Development history.* Before the benchmark we ran small development runs to build the instrument:
a feasibility pilot, two probe gates and two generation runs on D2. They used an earlier template, had gaps in the verifier, and
one probe was defective. Together with `{python} DZ["statistics"]["review_rounds"]` independent review rounds they shaped the instrument;
their numbers are not evidence. They cost `{python} usd(COST["development_spend_usd"], 2)`.

# Results {#sec-results}

## First iteration {#sec-first}


The first iteration asked `{python} V["n_gens"]` generators for one step-score
sheet per exam. Each step carried a weight class, ordered partial-credit levels, provenance and
consequential-error rules; alternative paths replaced named steps within their budget. A seeded
random draw fixed one valid sheet per exam for all judges. Judges graded the `{python} V["n_answers"]`
answers against the drawn sheet and, in matched arms, against the *holistic* instrument of the prior study
[@nagl2026bengerdata] (the same `{python} V["n_dims"]` dimensions for every exam) over `{python} passes` passes. A few-shot arm
regenerated sheets with one exemplar from another exam. We report totals as step sums: the first-iteration
pipeline sometimes stored the model's own total when it lay within half a point of the step sum
(Appendix \ref{sec-app-corrections}).

*Generation (RQ3).* `{python} V["n_valid"]` of `{python} V["n_cells"]` generator–exam cells hold a
valid sheet. `{python} V["n_full"]` generators covered every exam; Llama-4 Maverick covered
`{python} gen_s[llama]["valid"]` and GPT-5.4 Mini `{python} gen_s[MINI]["valid"]`, mostly because
feedback did not repair broken references of alternative paths. Of `{python} G["series_total"]`
dispatched series, `{python} G["series_failed"]` failed: `{python} G["failed_by_stage"]["provider"]`
aborted at the provider (all GPT-5.4 Mini, credit errors), `{python} G["failed_by_stage"]["contract"]`
failed validation and `{python} G["failed_by_stage"]["parse"]` failed parsing. First-attempt
compliance over all series that reached the model spans
`{python} pct(G["first_attempt_range_model_series"][0])` to
`{python} pct(G["first_attempt_range_model_series"][1])`. Counted over valid sheets only, GPT-5.4 Mini
looks better than it is: `{python} pct(gen_s[MINI]["first_attempt_rate_valid"])` there, but
`{python} pct(gen_s[MINI]["first_attempt_rate_model_series"])` over the series that reached the model
(`{python} gen_s[MINI]["first_attempt_successes"]` of `{python} gen_s[MINI]["model_series"]`) and
`{python} pct(gen_s[MINI]["first_attempt_rate_all_series"])` over all `{python} gen_s[MINI]["series"]`
of its series (Table \ref{tab:compliance}). Generators did not converge: mean step counts range from
`{python} num(G["step_count_mean_range"][0], 1)` to `{python} num(G["step_count_mean_range"][1], 1)`,
and stated weight sums from `{python} num(G["weight_sums"]["min"], 0)` to
`{python} num(G["weight_sums"]["max"], 0)`. A lexical screen found vague formulas that the prompt
itself bans in `{python} G["lexical_screen"]["listed"]` of `{python} G["lexical_screen"]["n_rubrics"]`
sheets (`{python} G["lexical_screen"]["any"]` with near variants). The generation prompt asked for
"exactly `{python} CONTRACT["bounds"]["total_points"]` raw points" in its first line, while its
weighting rule said that no exact sum was needed because code normalizes; we disclose this as an
ambiguity. The weight class was shown to the judge but played no part in the arithmetic.

```{python}
#| output: asis
LBL = {"holistic_luna": "Holistic", "tailored_luna": "Step-score sheet, zero-shot",
       "fewshot_luna": "Step-score sheet, few-shot", "holistic_mini": "Holistic",
       "tailored_mini": "Step-score sheet, zero-shot", "fewshot_mini": "Step-score sheet, few-shot"}
DAG = r"\textsuperscript{\textdagger}"


def rel_row(key):
    r = REL[key]
    if r["basis"] == "step_sum":
        return [LBL[key], num(r["repeat_sd"]), cor(r["r"]), num(r["mae"], 1), sgn(r["bias_stored"], 1) + DAG]
    if r["basis"] == "stored_pending":
        return [LBL[key], num(r["repeat_sd_stored"]) + DAG, cor(r["r_stored"]) + DAG,
                num(r["mae_stored"], 1) + DAG, sgn(r["bias_stored"], 1) + DAG]
    return [LBL[key], num(r["repeat_sd"]), cor(r["r"]), num(r["mae"], 1), sgn(r["bias"], 1)]


prs = FI["reliability"]["panel_sd_range"]
rows = [r"\multicolumn{5}{@{}l}{\emph{Judge: GPT-5.6 Luna}}"]
rows += [rel_row(k) for k in ("holistic_luna", "tailored_luna", "fewshot_luna")]
rows += ["MIDRULE", r"\multicolumn{5}{@{}l}{\emph{Judge: GPT-5.4 Mini}}"]
rows += [rel_row(k) for k in ("holistic_mini", "tailored_mini", "fewshot_mini")]
write_table(
    "tbl_reliability",
    f"First iteration: stability and agreement by instrument. SD\\textsubscript{{rep}}: repeat SD over "
    f"{passes} passes on {FI['reliability']['repeat_n']} answers. $r$, MAE, bias: first pass against the "
    f"human pool on {FI['reliability']['agreement_n']} human-written answers; bias is judge minus humans. "
    "Step-score totals are step sums. "
    + (f"{DAG}Stored total. " if any(REL[k]["basis"] in ("step_sum", "stored_pending") for k in REL) else "")
    + f"The {FI['reliability']['panel_size']}-judge panel SD ranges "
    f"from {num(prs[0])} to {num(prs[1])} across the panel definitions.",
    "tab:reliability", ["Instrument", "SD\\textsubscript{rep}", "$r$", "MAE", "bias"], rows,
    colspec="lrrrr", size=r"\footnotesize")
```

*Variance (RQ1).* For Luna, repeat SD falls from `{python} num(REL["holistic_luna"]["repeat_sd"])`
(holistic) to `{python} num(REL["tailored_luna"]["repeat_sd"])` (zero-shot sheet) and
`{python} num(REL["fewshot_luna"]["repeat_sd"])` (few-shot sheet;
Table \ref{tab:reliability}). The direction is consistent, but no single step is established:
few-shot minus holistic is `{python} sgn(lf["point"])` (`{python} ci(lf["ci95"])`; sign test
$p$ = `{python} pv(lf["sign_p"])`), zero-shot minus holistic `{python} sgn(lz["point"])`
(`{python} ci(lz["ci95"])`; $p$ = `{python} pv(lz["sign_p"])`), and few-shot minus zero-shot
`{python} sgn(lfz["point"])` (`{python} ci(lfz["ci95"])`; $p$ = `{python} num(lfz["sign_p"])`). Across
the `{python} V["n_matched"]` judges with matched arms, the zero-shot effect averages
`{python} sgn(pooled["point"])` (`{python} ci(pooled["ci95"])`; Table \ref{tab:contrasts}). This is the
unweighted mean of the per-judge differences, without correction for multiple comparisons. Only
Sonnet's per-judge interval excludes zero, and it points the adverse way: Claude Sonnet 4.6 is steadier with
the holistic instrument (`{python} sgn(son_f["delta"])`, `{python} ci(son_f["ci95"])`). Below the
capability floor the sheet destabilizes the judge: GPT-5.4 Mini's repeat SD rises from
`{python} num(REL["holistic_mini"]["repeat_sd"])` to `{python} num(REL["tailored_mini"]["repeat_sd"])`
(`{python} sgn(mini_f["delta"])`, `{python} ci(mini_f["ci95"])`, clustered by exam; cell-level sign
test $p$ = `{python} pv(mz["sign_p"])`, Wilcoxon $p$ = `{python} pv(mz["wilcoxon_p"])`). The steadiest
few-shot sheets, a post-hoc subset by generator, reached `{python} num(min(fs_sd.values()))` with
Luna, and an in-sample floor (the best sheet per exam, chosen after the fact)
`{python} num(CO["trend_luna"]["in_sample_floor"])`; both are optimistic bounds without intervals.
These contrasts use step sums; on the stored totals they differ by at most
`{python} num(CONTRAST_SHIFT)`.

*Agreement (RQ2).* Agreement with the human pool fell as the sheets tightened. Luna's $r$ moved from
`{python} cor(AG["luna"]["hol"]["r"])` to `{python} cor(AG["luna"]["zs_step_sum"]["r"])` and
`{python} cor(AG["luna"]["fs_stored"]["r"])`, and its bias flipped from
`{python} sgn(AG["luna"]["hol"]["bias"], 1)` to `{python} sgn(AG["luna"]["zs_bias_stored"], 1)` and
`{python} sgn(AG["luna"]["fs_stored"]["bias"], 1)`; the few-shot exemplars had been chosen for
stability alone. Its zero-shot MAE rose by `{python} sgn(AG["luna"]["mae_zs_minus_hol"]["point"], 1)`
(`{python} ci(AG["luna"]["mae_zs_minus_hol"]["ci95"], 1)`). GPT-5.4 Mini graded adequately with the
holistic instrument ($r$ = `{python} cor(AG["mini"]["hol"]["r"])`, MAE
`{python} num(AG["mini"]["hol"]["mae"], 1)`) but not with the sheet: $r$ =
`{python} cor(AG["mini"]["zs_step_sum"]["r"])`, MAE `{python} num(AG["mini"]["zs_step_sum"]["mae"], 1)`,
an increase of `{python} sgn(AG["mini"]["mae_zs_minus_hol"]["point"], 1)`
(`{python} ci(AG["mini"]["mae_zs_minus_hol"]["ci95"], 1)`). Few-shot sheets left it there ($r$ =
`{python} cor(AG["mini"]["fs_stored"]["r"])`, MAE `{python} num(AG["mini"]["fs_stored"]["mae"], 1)`).
Leave-one-exam-out bias correction shows that the error of the prior study's control judge was
mostly a level shift (MAE `{python} num(C["legacy_control"]["mae"], 1)` to
`{python} num(AG["loeo_calibrated_mae"]["holistic_control"], 1)`), whereas Luna's zero-shot error was
not (`{python} num(AG["luna"]["zs_step_sum"]["mae"], 1)` to
`{python} num(AG["loeo_calibrated_mae"]["tailored_luna"], 1)`).

*Judges and probes.* The `{python} len(JU["roster"])` roster judges graded all answers against the drawn sheets
(Table \ref{tab:judges}). Apart from Mini they reached $r$ `{python} cor(JU["capable_r_range"][0])`
to `{python} cor(JU["capable_r_range"][1])`; Claude Opus 5 and GPT-5.6 Terra, one pass each,
`{python} cor(extra["claude-opus-5"]["r"])` and `{python} cor(extra["gpt-5.6-terra"]["r"])`. A battery of
`{python} PR["n_probes_per_type"]` degenerate answers per type (the case text verbatim, a near-empty
answer, another exam's model solution) and each exam's own model solution as a positive control
tested execution (Table \ref{tab:probes}). Only `{python} " and ".join(NAME[j] for j in PR["clean_battery"])`
passed the negative battery on every pass. Luna credited the near-empty answer on
`{python} fc["tailored"][LUNA]["empty"]` of `{python} npas["tailored"][LUNA]["empty"]` zero-shot passes and
`{python} fc["fewshot"][LUNA]["empty"]` of `{python} npas["fewshot"][LUNA]["empty"]` few-shot passes, with
`{python} num(PR["luna_empty_mean_failing"]["tailored"], 1)` and
`{python} num(PR["luna_empty_mean_failing"]["fewshot"], 1)` points on average when it did (median
`{python} num(FL["luna_empty_median_failing"]["value"]["tailored"], 1)` and
`{python} num(FL["luna_empty_median_failing"]["value"]["fewshot"], 1)`), but on `{python} fc["holistic"][LUNA]["empty"]` holistic passes.
GPT-5.4 Mini failed `{python} PR["mini_negative_fails"]["tailored"]` of
`{python} PR["mini_negative_passes"]["tailored"]` negative passes under the sheet and
`{python} PR["mini_negative_fails"]["holistic"]` under the holistic instrument, but its holistic
failures were small (median `{python} num(sev["holistic"][MINI]["empty"]["median"], 0)` points on the
empty answer) and its sheet failures near-total (median
`{python} num(sev["tailored"][MINI]["empty"]["median"], 0)`). Under the sheet, the off-topic answer scored at most
`{python} num(max(v for j, v in PR["offtopic_max_tailored"].items() if j != MINI), 1)` points with every
judge except Mini (up to `{python} num(PR["offtopic_max_tailored"][MINI], 0)`). All
`{python} sum(1 for v in PR["positive_control"]["tailored"].values() if v == "pass")` judges passed the
positive control under the sheet; Mini failed it holistically on
`{python} PR["positive_control_fails"]["holistic"][MINI][0]` of
`{python} PR["positive_control_fails"]["holistic"][MINI][1]` passes. On one answer that only restates
the case, Mini under the sheet gave `{python} ", ".join(num(v, 0) for v in AG["p01"]["mini_zs"].values())`
points and Luna `{python} ", ".join(num(v, 0) for v in AG["p01"]["luna_zs"].values())`.

These failures belong to the first-iteration harness. It had no quote verification and a generic
system prompt. Its response schema listed the steps in storage order (by key length, then bytes),
not in outline order, and the steps of alternative paths had no response keys, so a judge had to
move credit for another path onto the replaced steps, where the per-step cap dropped any overflow
\pending{number of alternative paths affected}. Budget neutrality thus held in the document, not in
scoring. The new pipeline changes all of this at once. E0 and E2 must therefore measure the
capability floor again before we claim anything about it, and E4 can separate the levers only in
part.

*Generators and the audit (RQ4).* A crossed sweep graded each exam's answers under every valid sheet
of that exam: `{python} GE["n_rubrics"]` sheets and `{python} GE["n_rubric_pick_cells"]` sheet–answer
cells, Luna, `{python} passes` passes (Table \ref{tab:generators}). An automated audit by GPT-5.4 Mini
rated each blinded sheet on `{python} GE["audit"]["n_dimensions"]` dimensions from 1 to
`{python} GE["audit"]["scale_max"]`. Within exams, the audit total shows no linear association with
grading error ($r$ = `{python} cor(link["mae_centered"]["pearson"])`,
`{python} ci(link["mae_centered"]["ci95"])`; Spearman `{python} cor(link["mae_centered"]["spearman"])`)
and a weak one with stability ($r$ = `{python} cor(link["repeat_sd_centered"]["pearson"])`,
`{python} ci(link["repeat_sd_centered"]["ci95"])`; Spearman
`{python} cor(link["repeat_sd_centered"]["spearman"])`). It correlates with the *absolute* bias
($r$ = `{python} cor(link["abs_bias_centered"]["pearson"])`, `{python} ci(link["abs_bias_centered"]["ci95"])`)
and with the signed bias ($r$ = `{python} cor(FL["audit_signed_bias_link"]["value"]["pearson"])`,
`{python} ci(FL["audit_signed_bias_link"]["value"]["ci95"])`): higher-rated sheets grade harsher. At the generator level
($n$ = `{python} GE["generator_level_spearman_audit_vs_bias"]["n"]`), higher audit totals go with
harsher grading (Spearman `{python} cor(GE["generator_level_spearman_audit_vs_bias"]["luna"])` with
Luna, `{python} cor(GE["generator_level_spearman_audit_vs_bias"]["sonnet"])` with Sonnet): the Claude
sheets top the audit (`{python} num(gpo[opus]["audit_total"], 1)` and
`{python} num(gpo[sonnet]["audit_total"], 1)` of `{python} GE["audit"]["n_dimensions"] * GE["audit"]["scale_max"]`)
and grade among the harshest (bias `{python} sgn(gpo[opus]["bias"], 1)` and `{python} sgn(gpo[sonnet]["bias"], 1)`).
DeepSeek-V4-Flash sheets cut agreement ($r$ = `{python} cor(gpo[dsf]["validity_r"])`, the lowest)
behind a mid-field audit (`{python} num(gpo[dsf]["audit_total"], 1)`). Llama-4 Maverick sheets made
Luna least stable (repeat SD `{python} num(gpo[llama]["repeat_sd_mean"])`), but the audit ranked them
lowest (`{python} num(gpo[llama]["audit_total"], 1)`), so this failure was visible. GPT-5.4 Mini, the
weakest judge and least compliant generator, wrote the best sheets when it wrote any (paired
$\Delta$MAE `{python} sgn(gpo[MINI]["paired_dmae"], 1)` on `{python} gpo[MINI]["n_rubrics"]` exams), but
its probability of ranking first is `{python} cor(mini_rank["p_top1"])` and the estimate is conditional
on survival. The ranking replicates moderately under a Sonnet lens (Spearman
`{python} cor(GE["lens_spearman"])`; `{python} cor(GE["lens_spearman_full_coverage"])` among
full-coverage generators). Few-shot generation raised Mini's valid sheets from
`{python} G["zeroshot_compliance_mini"]["valid"]` to `{python} G["fewshot_compliance"][MINI]["valid"]` of
`{python} G["fewshot_compliance"][MINI]["total"]`; since the few-shot arm also used its own pool of
`{python} V["n_fs_gens"]` generators, its effects are confounded with that pool.

*Weights and step size.* The generated weights carry a small, judge-dependent signal
(Appendix \ref{sec-app-weights}). Re-aggregating the stored per-step scores, Luna keeps most of its agreement with
class weights alone ($r$ `{python} cor(ws_j[LUNA]["class_only"]["r"], 3)` vs
`{python} cor(ws_j[LUNA]["actual"]["r"], 3)`) and loses some with uniform weights
(`{python} cor(ws_j[LUNA]["uniform"]["r"], 3)`). For DeepSeek-V4-Pro, class weights do worse than uniform
ones (`{python} cor(ws_j["deepseek-ai/DeepSeek-V4-Pro"]["class_only"]["r"], 3)` vs
`{python} cor(ws_j["deepseek-ai/DeepSeek-V4-Pro"]["uniform"]["r"], 3)`). Uniform weights lowered repeat
SD for `{python} len(ws_s["uniform_lowers_repeat_sd"])` of `{python} ws_s["n_judges"]` judges, and the
actual weights beat `{python} num(100 * ws_s["perm_share_range"][0], 0)` to
`{python} pct(ws_s["perm_share_range"][1])` of within-sheet permutations. The judges saw the actual step
maxima, so these re-aggregations are conditional on them. Step size matters more than step count
(Appendix \ref{sec-app-steps}). Steps of `{python} SS["summary"]["bucket"]` points held
`{python} pct(ss[LUNA]["share_points"])` of the points but a larger share of the summed per-step
variance for `{python} len(SS["summary"]["disproportionate"])` judges: Luna `{python} pct(ss[LUNA]["share_variance"])`, Gemini
`{python} pct(ss["gemini-3.1-pro-preview"]["share_variance"])`, Sonnet
`{python} pct(ss[sonnet]["share_variance"], 1)`, DeepSeek-V4-Pro
`{python} pct(ss["deepseek-ai/DeepSeek-V4-Pro"]["share_variance"])`, and Opus 4.7
`{python} pct(ss[opus]["share_variance"])` from `{python} pct(ss[opus]["share_points"])` of its points
(`{python} ss[opus]["n_step_cells"]` step cells). For Qwen
(`{python} pct(ss["Qwen/Qwen3.5-397B-A17B"]["share_variance"])`) and Mini
(`{python} pct(ss[MINI]["share_variance"])`) the share was close to proportional. Across the
`{python} GE["granularity"]["n_rubrics"]` sheets, step count correlated only weakly with error
($r$ = `{python} cor(GE["granularity"]["steps_vs_mae_r"])`) and with repeat SD
(`{python} cor(GE["granularity"]["steps_vs_repeat_sd_r"])`). The new instrument therefore uses small
steps and tests step size as a lever.

## Preliminary results on the expert exam {#sec-prelim}

```{python}
#| output: false
def _load(name):
    f = PROC / "cslaw" / name
    return json.loads(f.read_text(encoding="utf-8")) if f.exists() else None


GATE2 = _load("gate_v2.json")
GEN2 = _load("d2_generation.json")
VAL2 = _load("d2_validity.json")
INSTR = {"expert sheet:step": "Expert sheet (step unit)",
         "gpt-5.4 sheet 1:bullet": "GPT-5.4 checklist sheet",
         "gpt-5.4-mini sheet 1:bullet": "GPT-5.4 Mini checklist sheet 1",
         "gpt-5.4-mini sheet 2:bullet": "GPT-5.4 Mini checklist sheet 2"}
JUDGES_ORDER = ["gpt-5.6-luna", "deepseek-ai/DeepSeek-V4-Pro", "gpt-5.4-mini"]

```

These runs are a first look at the expert exam, not the benchmark: the pipeline as it stood
(output specification checklist-3), sheets from two generators, and up to three judges. They include
no run without a sheet, so they speak to validity
(RQ2) and generation (RQ3), not yet to variance reduction (RQ1). The reference grades of
`{python} D2["d2a"]["n_scripts"]` D2a scripts serve as the yardstick; the exam author has yet to
confirm who graded `{python} D2["d2a"]["grader_pending"]` of them, so we call them reference grades, not expert grades.

```{python}
#| output: asis
def _gen_par():
    a, b = GG.get("gpt-5.4"), GG.get("gpt-5.4-mini")
    if not (a and b):
        return r"*Generation.* \pending{generation summary}"
    steps = lambda g: " and ".join(str(x) for x in g["valid_sheet_steps"])
    ends = {}
    for g in (a, b):
        for k, v in g["failed_chain_final_categories"].items():
            ends[k] = ends.get(k, 0) + v
    n_failed = (a["chains"] - a["valid_sheets"]) + (b["chains"] - b["valid_sheets"])
    coarse = [i + 1 for i, d in enumerate(b["valid_sheet_detail"]) if d["hints"].get("gewicht")]
    return (
        f"*Generation.* GPT-5.4 produced a valid sheet in {a['valid_sheets']} of {a['chains']} chains "
        f"({steps(a)} steps), GPT-5.4 Mini in {b['valid_sheets']} of {b['chains']} ({steps(b)} steps"
        + (f"; the validator flagged sheet {coarse[0]} as coarse" if coarse else "") + "). "
        f"Of the {n_failed} failed chains, {ends.get('gewicht (10 BE cap)', 0)} ended on the 10-BE cap, "
        f"{ends.get('weichenstellungen', 0)} on the rules for forks and {ends.get('unparseable response', 0)} "
        "on an unreadable response. GPT-5.4 builds richer alternative paths, and "
        f"{a['failed_attempt_categories'].get('weichenstellungen', 0)} of its "
        f"{a['failed_attempts']} failed attempts broke the rules on forks. For GPT-5.4 Mini, {b['failed_attempt_categories'].get('gewicht (10 BE cap)', 0)} "
        f"of {b['failed_attempts']} failed attempts exceeded the cap: a generator states relative weights, "
        "not BE, and on a solution path only splitting a step helps, which the feedback did not say. A "
        f"valid sheet cost {usd(a['usd_per_valid_sheet'], 2)} with GPT-5.4 and {usd(b['usd_per_valid_sheet'], 2)} "
        "with GPT-5.4 Mini, failed chains included.")
print(_gen_par())
```

*Probe battery.* Luna (`{python} min(x["complete_passes"] for per in GATE2["batteries"].values() for j, x in per.items() if j == "gpt-5.6-luna")`
passes) and DeepSeek (`{python} min(x["complete_passes"] for per in GATE2["batteries"].values() for j, x in per.items() if j != "gpt-5.6-luna")`;
its second pass stopped for time) passed the battery on every instrument they were gated on (Table
\ref{tab:gate2}): no degenerate answer received points. The plan asks for `{python} DZ["probes"]["passes"]` passes, and
GPT-5.4 Mini as a judge and the second GPT-5.4 Mini sheet were not gated; their rows in Table
\ref{tab:val2} are marked. Removing one
part of the model solution cost about as many points as the sheet assigns to that part, and moving
a correct paragraph under another heading cost almost nothing. On the
expert sheet in the step unit, Luna still proposed half a point for every step of an empty or
off-topic answer, and only the rule that a credit needs a quote removed them; on the checklist
sheets it proposed nothing in the first place.

```{python}
    "$^\\dagger$ not gated by the probe battery.",
    "tab:val2",
    ["Instrument", "Judge", "Passes", "MAE [95\\% CI]", "Bias", "$r$", "Agr.", "$\\kappa$", "SD\\textsubscript{rep}"],
    vrows or [[r"\tbd"] * 9], colspec="llrrrrrrr", size=r"\footnotesize", wide=True)
```

```{python}
#| output: asis
def _v(arm, judge):
    return ((VAL2 or {}).get("per_arm", {}).get(arm, {}) or {}).get(judge)


def _c(a, b):
    for c in (VAL2 or {}).get("contrasts", []):
        if (c["a"]["judge"], c["a"]["arm"]) == a and (c["b"]["judge"], c["b"]["arm"]) == b:
            return c
    return None


def _d(x, nd=1):
    """A paired difference with its bootstrap interval."""
    return f"{sgn(x['mean_diff'], nd)} [{num(x['ci95'][0], nd)}, {num(x['ci95'][1], nd)}]"


LU, MI, DSK, EXS = "gpt-5.6-luna", "gpt-5.4-mini", "deepseek-ai/DeepSeek-V4-Pro", "expert sheet:step"
G54, M1, M2 = "gpt-5.4 sheet 1:bullet", "gpt-5.4-mini sheet 1:bullet", "gpt-5.4-mini sheet 2:bullet"
_lx, _mx, _dx = _v(EXS, LU), _v(EXS, MI), _v(EXS, DSK)
_lg, _lm, _dg = _v(G54, LU), _v(M1, LU), _v(G54, DSK)
_cj, _cg, _cm, _cw = _c((MI, EXS), (LU, EXS)), _c((LU, G54), (LU, EXS)), _c((LU, M1), (LU, EXS)), _c((MI, EXS), (LU, G54))
if not all((_lx, _mx, _lg, _lm, _cj, _cg, _cm, _cw)):
    print(r"*Agreement with the reference grades.* \pending{validity runs}")
else:
    parts = [
        "*Agreement with the reference grades.* On the expert's own sheet, a single Luna pass came "
        f"within {num(_lx['mae'], 1)} points of the reference grades on average (bias {sgn(_lx['bias'], 1)}, "
        f"$r$ = {cor(_lx['pearson'])}) and agreed on pass or fail for {pct(_lx['pass_agreement'])} of the "
        f"scripts ($\\kappa$ = {cor(_lx['pass_kappa'])}); two passes differed by {num(_lx['mean_abs_pass_diff'], 1)} "
        f"points on average (Table \\ref{{tab:val2}}). GPT-5.4 Mini, the platform's current default judge, was "
        f"further off on the same sheet (MAE {num(_mx['mae'], 1)}, $r$ = {cor(_mx['pearson'])}); paired over the "
        f"scripts, the difference in absolute error was {_d(_cj['abs_error'])}.",
    ]
    if _dx:
        parts.append(
            f"DeepSeek-V4-Pro reached an MAE of {num(_dx['mae'], 1)} on the expert sheet"
            + (f" and {num(_dg['mae'], 1)} on the GPT-5.4 sheet." if _dg else "."))
    parts.append(
        f"With generated sheets, Luna's MAE was {num(_lg['mae'], 1)} (GPT-5.4 sheet) and "
        f"{num(_lm['mae'], 1)} (GPT-5.4 Mini sheet 1). The change is mostly leniency: the signed error "
        f"rose by {_d(_cg['signed_error'])} and {_d(_cm['signed_error'])} points, the absolute error by "
        f"{_d(_cg['abs_error'])} and {_d(_cm['abs_error'])}, while the order of the scripts stayed close to "
        f"the reference ($r$ = {cor(_lg['pearson'])} and {cor(_lm['pearson'])}).")
    parts.append(
        "Two readings follow, both preliminary. First, the judge mattered at least as much as the sheet: "
        "the default judge on the expert's sheet was not closer to the reference than Luna on the GPT-5.4 "
        f"sheet (difference {_d(_cw['abs_error'])}). Second, the generated sheets were more lenient than "
        "the expert's; a generated sheet needs a stricter specification or a calibration step before its "
        "totals can stand in for an examiner's.")
    _ss = ((VAL2 or {}).get("sheet_sample", {}).get("gpt-5.4-mini:bullet", {}) or {}).get(LU)
    _l2 = _v(M2, LU)
    if _ss and _l2:
        parts.append(
            f"A second GPT-5.4 Mini sheet from the same input gave Luna an MAE of {num(_l2['mae'], 1)} "
            f"(bias {sgn(_l2['bias'], 1)}). A script's total differed between the two sheets by "
            f"{num(_ss['mean_abs_sheet_diff'], 1)} points on average. Separating the pass noise, the "
            f"sheet-to-sheet SD is {num(_ss['sheet_sd_component'], 1)} and the pass-to-pass SD "
            f"{num(_ss['pass_sd_pooled'], 1)}: "
            + ("the sheet a generator happens to write adds variance of the same order as the judge's own noise"
               if _ss["sheet_sd_component"] <= 1.5 * _ss["pass_sd_pooled"] else
               "the sheet a generator happens to write adds more variance than the judge's own noise")
            + ", so a benchmark has to sample several sheets per generator.")
    print(" ".join(parts), end="")
    _mdes = [c["abs_error"]["mde"] for c in (VAL2 or {}).get("contrasts", []) if c["abs_error"].get("mde")]
    print(
        f" With {D2['d2a']['n_scripts']} scripts of one exam, the observed paired spread puts the smallest "
        f"detectable difference in absolute error at {num(min(_mdes), 1)} to {num(max(_mdes), 1)} points "
        "(80\\% power, $\\alpha$ = .05): these are first signals, not a ranking.")
```

## Benchmark results (E1 to E7)

\pending{E1 to E7}. E1 reports per generator compliance, validator defects, the author's spot audit
of `{python} EXP["E1"]["audit_bullets_per_sheet"]` bullets per sheet, validity, repeat and
sheet-sample SD, and cost per valid sheet; E2 per judge validity against the expert (incl. ICC(A,1)
and pass/fail $\kappa$), per-step agreement, repeat SD, the probe battery and cost. E3 estimates
variance components and rank stability across judges, E4 the Pareto front of error, variance and
cost with one confirmation on D2b, E5 the designs for alternative paths; E6 and E7 answer
@sec-practice.

# Discussion {#sec-discussion}

\draftnote{the answers per research question are written after E1 to E7}

*What the first iteration already shows.* First, a generated sheet does not reduce variance by
itself. Whether it steadies a judge depends on the judge and the sheet together: across the capable
judges the average effect was null, and one judge was steadier without a sheet. Second, mean
agreement hides a failure that matters for every grade a student sees. Under detailed sheets, some
judges gave near-full credit to empty and copied answers far more often than with the holistic
instrument (@sec-first). A probe
battery must therefore gate every judge and instrument before use, and code must tie every credit to
the answer. Third, writing, using and auditing a sheet are different skills. The least compliant
generator wrote the best sheets when it succeeded, and the automated audit favoured sheets that
graded harshly. Generator and judge must be chosen together, by outcome.

*Answers to the research questions.* \pending{one paragraph per research question after E1 to E7}

*Implications for practice.* The pipeline is a research instrument. Its sheets make each credit
auditable: an examiner can see which requirement a quote met and can correct the sheet itself, which
a holistic score does not allow. Two uses fit the evidence so far: checkable feedback on practice
exams, and drafts that examiners edit rather than trust. Grade-bearing assessment needs a human
examiner.
\pending{recommended pipeline and its cost per script}

# Limitations {#sec-limitations}

*One expert exam.* D2 is one case in one area of law, graded on its author's sheet. D1 spans many exams, but
its human reference is noisy. Results on D2 may not transfer to other exams, areas or examiners, and
the second grader gives a human ceiling for one exam only.

*Open data questions.* For `{python} D2["d2a"]["grader_pending"]` D2a scripts the grader is not yet
confirmed, and the `{python} D2["d2a"]["later_case_text"]` scripts of 2024 are judged against a later
year's case text. The judge sees the current sheet also for scripts graded on an earlier state. The D2b students saw LLM grades before the author grades their scripts; he grades without
seeing them.

*The exam author is a co-author.* He wrote the exam, grades the scripts, audits generated sheets and
co-writes this paper, so he knows the study's aims. Blind grading of D2b and the second grader limit
this, but his spot audit of generated sheets is not independent.

*Leakage.* During development, examples in the generator and judge prompts came from the D2 exam.
We replaced them with neutral examples and added a canary check. The check is lexical and cannot
rule out that the prompts were shaped while the expert sheet was in hand.

*Verification.* The verifier checks that a quote exists, not that it supports the credit
(@sec-verifier). It rejects some correct quotes and cannot catch a real sentence quoted for the
wrong requirement.

*Models and sampling.* GPT-5.6 Luna cannot be seeded. Even at temperature 0, DeepSeek-V4-Pro's
totals varied between passes (repeat SD `{python} num(roster["deepseek-ai/DeepSeek-V4-Pro"]["repeat_sd"])`
in the first iteration), so repeat SD mixes model, sampling and serving effects. Providers change and retire models; we record model ids and
dates. The prior study's repeat baseline ran on a retired judge; no contrast we interpret uses it.

*Exploratory design.* Nothing was pre-registered and many comparisons are reported
(@sec-experiments). The confirmation on D2b is used once. Several first-iteration arms were added
after earlier results were known.

# Ethics {#sec-ethics}

*Consent and personal data.* The students whose D2 scripts we use consented to research use, for the
`{python} D2["d2a"]["n_scripts"]` scripts of D2a and the `{python} D2["d2b"]["n_uploads"]` platform
submissions of D2b. The consent does not extend to sending their personal data to model providers.
All D2 texts are therefore pseudonymized and checked for personal data before any research call
(@sec-d2). The platform grades that the D2b students saw were produced in the normal use of the
platform, before this study. \pending{owner to confirm the wording on the platform-side grading and the providers' data terms}
D1 reuses the prior study's corpus under the consent obtained there, with pseudonymized graders
[@nagl2026bengerdata].

*Roles.* The exam author is a co-author, the source of the reference grades and the auditor of
generated sheets. We report this as a limitation and mitigate it with blind grading and a second
grader.

*Students who saw LLM grades.* The D2b students received LLM grades as feedback on a practice exam.
\pending{owner: whether and how students learn the expert grades}

*Use of the instrument.* Generated sheets are studied as a research instrument for evaluating and
supporting grading. They are not a replacement for human examiners in grade-bearing assessment, where
legal and pedagogical safeguards apply.

*Roth's sheet.* Gregor Roth agreed to be named and to have his sheet and workbook used. We report
only their structure, not their content.

# Data and code availability {#sec-availability}

The platform, including the judge, the verifier and the aggregation code, is open source at
<https://github.com/SebastianNagl/benger-platform>. Its folder `publications/Transformation` holds the
analysis scripts and every aggregate this paper reports (`make analyze-cslaw`; the D2 and Z2
aggregates need the private data, `make analyze-d2`). The generator is part of a proprietary extension of the
platform. \pending{owner decision: release of the generator prompt, output specification and validator rules}
D1's exam texts are third-party material and are not redistributed, nor are the generated sheets,
which enumerate the model solutions. D2 and Roth's sheet are private, and we publish only aggregates
(Appendix \ref{sec-app-datastatement}).

# AI usage {#sec-ai}

For the first iteration the authors used OpenAI GPT-5.6 Sol to discuss approaches and Anthropic
Claude Fable 5 for coding and writing assistance. For the extended study, Anthropic Claude Opus 5.5
was used for coding, for `{python} DZ["statistics"]["review_rounds"]` independent review rounds of the
instrument and the analysis, and for writing assistance,
including an AI-assisted literature scan. All results were verified by the authors, and all
citations were checked against their sources. The authors take full responsibility for the paper.

# Apportionment audit {#sec-app-apportionment}

The audit re-derives the points of all `{python} AP["n_rubrics"]` first-iteration sheets
(`{python} AP["n_steps"]` steps) from their stated weights under each routine of Table
\ref{tab:apportionment}. A step lies outside its fair range when its points differ from its quota by
a full unit or more; an order inversion is a pair in which the lighter step receives more points.
The as-run routine is reproduced exactly by a copy of the original code.

```{python}
#| output: asis
MLBL = {"as_run": "As run (first iteration)", "hamilton_floor": "Hamilton, floor first (integer)",
        "hamilton_half": "Hamilton, floor first (half points)"}
arows = []
for k in ("as_run", "hamilton_floor", "hamilton_half"):
    m = AP[k]
    arows.append([MLBL[k], m["steps_outside_fair_range"], m["rubrics_outside_fair_range"], m["order_inversion_pairs"],
                  m["collapsed_distinct_weight_pairs"], num(m["rel_error_median"], 3), m["steps_changed_vs_as_run"]])
write_table(
    "tbl_apportionment",
    f"Apportionment of the {AP['n_rubrics']} first-iteration sheets under three routines: steps outside their "
    "fair range, sheets affected, order-inversion pairs, pairs of distinct weights that receive equal points, "
    "median relative rounding error, and steps whose points differ from the as-run result.",
    "tab:apportionment", ["Routine", "Steps", "Sheets", "Inversions", "Collapsed", "Rel. error", "Changed"],
    arows, size=r"\footnotesize")
```

# Weight sensitivity {#sec-app-weights}

Every first-iteration judgment stores a score and a maximum per step. Re-weighting the stored
fractions shows how much the generated allocation contributes to agreement and stability without new
judge calls (Table \ref{tab:weights}). *Actual* reproduces the step sums; *class* weights each step by its
weight class (routine `{python} num(WS["summary"]["class_weights"]["routine"], 0)`, load-bearing
`{python} num(WS["summary"]["class_weights"]["tragend"], 0)`, focal `{python} num(WS["summary"]["class_weights"]["schwerpunkt"], 0)`); *uniform* counts every step the same; *permuted* shuffles a sheet's own
points across its steps. The judges saw the actual maxima, so every scheme is conditional on them.

```{python}
#| output: asis
wrows = []
for j in sorted(ws_j, key=lambda j: NAME[j]):
    w = ws_j[j]
    wrows.append([NAME[j], cor(w["actual"]["r"], 3), cor(w["model_weights"]["r"], 3), cor(w["class_only"]["r"], 3),
                  cor(w["uniform"]["r"], 3), cor(w["sqrt_points"]["r"], 3),
                  pct(w["permuted"]["share_of_permutations_below_actual_r"]),
                  num(w["actual"]["repeat_sd"]), num(w["uniform"]["repeat_sd"])])
write_table(
    "tbl_weights",
    "Weight sensitivity of the first-iteration sheets: agreement $r$ with the human pool under five weight "
    "schemes, the share of within-sheet permutations whose $r$ falls below the actual one, and repeat SD under "
    "the actual and uniform weights.",
    "tab:weights", ["Judge", "Actual", "Model", "Class", "Uniform", "$\\sqrt{\\text{pts}}$", "Perm.",
                    "SD act.", "SD unif."],
    wrows, size=r"\footnotesize\setlength{\tabcolsep}{4pt}")
```

# Step size and variance {#sec-app-steps}

For every judge with at least `{python} passes` passes per answer, we sum the per-step variance across passes by
step size and compare it with the share of points in that size class (Table \ref{tab:steps}). The
share ignores covariance between steps, so it is a share of *summed* step variance. We call a size
class disproportionate when its share of variance exceeds its share of points by more than a factor
of `{python} num(SS["summary"]["ratio_threshold"], 1)`.

```{python}
#| output: asis
srows = []
for j in sorted(ss, key=lambda j: -ss[j]["ratio"]):
    v = ss[j]
    srows.append([NAME[j], v["n_cells"], v["n_step_cells"], pct(v["share_points"], 1), pct(v["share_variance"], 1),
                  num(v["ratio"])])
write_table(
    "tbl_steps",
    f"Steps of {SS['summary']['bucket']} points in the first-iteration sheets: answers and step cells, share "
    "of points, share of summed per-step repeat variance, and their ratio.",
    "tab:steps", ["Judge", "Answers", "Step cells", "Points", "Variance", "Ratio"], srows, size=r"\footnotesize")
```

# Precision {#sec-app-precision}

The minimum detectable effect of a paired contrast is
$(t_{1-\alpha/2,\,n-1} + t_{\text{power},\,n-1})\,\sigma_d/\sqrt{n}$. We take $\sigma_d$ from the
closest existing contrast, Luna with the zero-shot sheet vs the holistic instrument on D1, so the
values are planning proxies (Table \ref{tab:mde}). The D2 proxy uses a holistic human reference,
which is noisier than per-step expert grades; the first D2a runs show smaller spreads, and
@sec-prelim reports the detectable differences they imply.

```{python}
#| output: asis
c1, c2 = MDE["C1_repeat_sd"], MDE["C2_abs_error_vs_expert"]
NLBL = {"n_15_d2a": f"D2a ({D2['d2a']['n_scripts']} scripts)",
        "n_38_all_distinct": f"all distinct D2 scripts ({D2['distinct_scripts']})",
        "n_37_dependent_pair_once": f"D2, dependent pair once ({D2['n_counting_dependent_pair_once']})"}
mrows = [["Repeat SD, D1", c1["n"], num(c1["sd_of_differences"]), num(c1["mde"]["alpha_0.025"]), num(c1["mde"]["alpha_0.05"])],
         [f"Repeat SD, D1, {int(next(k for k in c1 if k.startswith('mde_') and 'passes' in k).split('_')[1])} passes (optimistic)", c1["n"], "",
          num(c1["mde_5_passes_optimistic"]["alpha_0.025"]), num(c1["mde_5_passes_optimistic"]["alpha_0.05"])]]
for k, lbl in NLBL.items():
    m = c2["mde"][k]
    mrows.append([f"Absolute error, {lbl}", "", num(c2["sd_of_differences"], 1), num(m["alpha_0.025"], 1),
                  num(m["alpha_0.05"], 1)])
write_table(
    "tbl_mde",
    f"Minimum detectable effects at power {cor(DZ['statistics']['mde_power'], 1)} ($t$-based, paired). "
    "$\\sigma_d$: SD of the paired differences in the proxy contrast.",
    "tab:mde", ["Contrast", "$n$", "$\\sigma_d$", "$\\alpha$ = .025", "$\\alpha$ = .05"], mrows,
    colspec="lrrrr", size=r"\footnotesize")
```
